cards.back: For each token the GPU reads every weight from memory. Serving 16 requests in one pass reads the same weights, and the extra maths is cheap, so throughput rises many times over.
When may a waiting request join a batch? Static, dynamic and in-flight batching give three different answers.
Collect a fixed number of requests, run them together and return everything when the last one finishes. Good for offline jobs, bad for live traffic.
Wasted slots grow with the spread of lengths in a batch, so sort the job by length before batching.

cards.front: Provider batch API vs GPU batching
cards.back: A provider's batch API is a job queue at about half price for jobs that can wait up to a day; the provider still schedules the GPUs however it likes.
Wait a short set time after the first request, gather others, then run what you have; run early if the batch fills. Suits fixed-size work like embedders and rerankers.
The maximum wait, usually a few milliseconds or less. Longer waits form bigger batches but add up to that wait to every request.
Schedules one generation step at a time: after every step finished requests leave and queued ones take their slots, so short answers don't wait for long ones.
Long prompts are processed in chunks so one big prefill doesn't stall everyone else's next token.

cards.front: What usually caps the batch size?
cards.back: KV cache memory, not compute: every active request holds its context there. Quantizing weights or the KV cache frees room for more requests.

quiz.q: You need to score a million documents overnight. Which scheduler fits?
quiz.why: Static batching suits offline jobs where everything is available up front and no user is waiting.

quiz.q: Why is dynamic batching a poor fit for LLM generation?
choices: It never waits for a batch to fill
Requests finish at different steps, so the batch waits for its longest answer
It needs a paged KV cache
quiz.why: Like static batching, a dynamic batch still holds slots until its longest answer ends.

quiz.q: In-flight batching depends on which piece of memory management?
quiz.why: Requests join and leave every step, so the KV cache must grow and free per request without fragmenting memory.

quiz.q: A RAG agent has an embedder, a reranker and an LLM. What's the usual setup?
choices: Dynamic for the LLM, in-flight for the embedder
Dynamic for embedder and reranker, in-flight for the LLM
quiz.why: One system often uses two schedulers: dynamic for fixed-size models and in-flight for generation.

quiz.q: A few long-context requests slow down every user's next token. What helps?
quiz.why: Long prompts make prefill heavy; chunking it keeps decode steps flowing for everyone else.

quiz.q: Raising the dynamic batching max wait from 2 ms to 20 ms mostly does what?
choices: Forms bigger batches but adds up to 20 ms per request
quiz.why: A longer wait trades added latency for bigger batches and more throughput.
